title: Atomic Weight Transaction Log for Rolling Updates
content:
Summary:

This doc proposes a transaction-log (WAL) based approach for performing atomic, multi-layer weight updates and rolling model upgrades across a distributed serving fleet. The core idea is to treat weight activation swaps as transactions recorded in a durable, append-only log so that nodes can perform coordinated, crash-safe rollouts without global locks or long pauses.

Motivation / Problems we want to solve:
- Enable zero-downtime model rollouts that update many tensor shards across GPUs and hosts while maintaining inference correctness.
- Avoid long global pause during weight swaps (hot-swap) and eliminate pathological failure modes where partial swaps leave nodes in inconsistent states.
- Provide a clear recovery path for interrupted rollouts (node crash, disk issues, partial fetch failures).
- Make on-disk weight artifacts (safetensors/mmap blobs) interoperate with transactional activation while keeping KV cache semantics correct.

Non-goals:
- Replacing coarse-grained replication or full-service orchestration. This complements existing rollout systems rather than replacing them.
- Defining new serialization formats beyond conservative use of safetensors + small transaction metadata files.

Design overview:
- We introduce an append-only Atomic Weight Transaction Log (AWTL). Each transaction declares a set of shard moves/activations and a small manifest that describes new artifact versions, checksums, preferred kernel variants (float16/8/quant), and optional patch deltas.
- Nodes tail the AWTL (via a push or poll mechanism) and attempt to apply transactions locally using a three-phase local protocol (prepare -> apply -> commit) with idempotent steps and durable markers on disk.
- Weight artifacts remain standard safetensors or mmap-backed blobs on fast local storage. The log stores references (URIs) + per-shard checksums and byte ranges.
- Local activation is implemented with an "activation journal" per node that mirrors the transaction log entries actually applied; this provides quick detection of partially applied transactions and enables replay/rollback.

Transaction record (manifest) format (high level):
- tx_id: monotonic UUID
- created_by: rollout controller id
- timestamp
- shards: list of { shard_id, uri, size_bytes, checksum, byte_range (optional), kernel_hint }
- prereqs: optional list of tx_ids this tx depends on
- post_actions: optional directives (invalidate-kv-prefixes, warmup-prefetch, kernel-flags)
- signature: controller signature (optional for private deployment)

Local state machine per transaction (idempotent steps):
1) PREPARE: fetch manifests for all shards listed. Validate checksums for any already-cached blobs. Allocate local temp files or mmap regions. Write a local prepare marker (prepare_<txid>) to local journal (fsync).
2) FETCH: concurrently download shard blobs into temporary locations; support ranged downloads for large blobs. For mmap artifacts we create a .pending symlink that points to the new file path. Maintain per-shard checksum verification. Retries are backoff-based; failed fetches report to controller.
3) VALIDATE: run lightweight sanity checks: tensor shapes, dtype, kernel_hint compatibility. Optionally run a small local smoke forward using a pinned prompt to ensure the layer integrates (configurable in canaries).
4) APPLY: atomically swap activation pointers. Implementation note: we do not copy entire weight files. Instead, serving processes refer to a lightweight activation manifest that maps logical layer -> filepath + offset + checksum + epoch. Swapping is a rename/symlink update plus an fsync and a write of apply_<txid> journal marker. Because the serving runtime looks up activation manifest entries in-memory, we provide an atomic in-memory switch via an index table update followed by a persist marker.
5) COMMIT: mark tx as committed in local journal (commit_<txid>), and notify controller. Optionally trigger background eviction of replaced blobs. If node is configured to be conservative, it may wait to see a quorum of peers commit before marking committed.

Crash recovery and idempotency:
- The local activation journal is the source of truth for partial work. On startup, a node scans for prepare_/apply_/commit_ markers and replays incomplete transactions: incomplete FETCH -> retry fetch; prepared but not applied -> attempt APPLY; applied but uncommitted -> COMMIT. All steps are idempotent (re-downloading overwrites temp files, re-applying swaps checks epoch).
- To avoid dangling mmap handles, apply uses a short, per-process grace window: new activation manifests are published, the runtime allows in-flight requests to drain from old KV cache epoch then switches. A background janitor unlinks stale files after last-FD-close detection (or after a configured GC grace period).

Mmap + safetensors interplay:
- Artifact URIs may point to safetensors archives, but nodes prefer mmap-able files for low-latency lazy load. When a safetensors archive is present, we support a two-path approach: (A) direct mmap of a pre-converted safetensors binary that already contains contiguous tensors optimized for mmap; (B) on-first-deploy, a converter step transforms safetensors->mmap-friendly layout into a sibling file with checksums recorded in the tx manifest. The converter writes into the temp location used by FETCH to ensure atomic activation.
- To support constrained disk, the fetcher supports streamed mmap-backed write that writes page-aligned chunks and fsyncs periodically to allow early memory-mapping of already-written pages for long tensors.

KV cache compatibility and decoupling:
- The KV cache is a separate logical cache keyed by model-version + sequence-prefix fingerprint. We avoid invalidating KV caches aggressively during activations by introducing a soft-lease scheme: each activation has an epoch id; KV entries are labeled with the epoch they were populated under. When an activation swaps, KV entries with older epochs are considered "stale" but usable for prefetched prefixes; correctness requires either conservative invalidation of dependent prefixes or safe fallback to compute-from-scratch when needed.
- Post-activation, a background validator can probabilistically validate KV entries: replay a small set of canonical prompts and compare outputs to ensure no silent regressions; flagged prefixes can be invalidated.

Eviction and prioritization heuristics:
- We prioritize eviction of replaced artifacts with low-access counters and large disk footprints first. Priority score = alpha * last_access_recency + beta * (1 / request_rate) + gamma * (size_bytes). Tunable weights.
- For rolling upgrades, do not evict old artifacts immediately: keep them around until a node confirms commit and, for a configurable grace period, until controller signals all downstream callers have observed new version (via canary traffic).

Rollout choreography (controller responsibilities):
- Generate tx manifest and publish to cluster log.
- Optionally include phased traffic directives: {phase1: subset hosts, canary_percent, prefetch:true, smoke_test:true}.
- For each phase, wait for at least N successful commits and green smoke tests before expanding.
- On failures, push a compensating tx (rollback) or instruct nodes to abort via the log (abort_<txid>).

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Partial disk full during FETCH: nodes detect insufficient space during PREPARE and report back. Controller can allocate alternative hosts or instruct staggered rollout.
- Corrupt download / checksum mismatch: fail-fetch and retry with exponential backoff; after X attempts, mark node unhealthy.
- Mmap file open by runtime prevents immediate unlink: use GC grace window and reference-counted file tracking to unlink only after last-FD-close.
- Divergent kernel_hint across shards: validate at tx creation; if mismatch occurs, controller can schedule a separate kernel-variant rollout.

Observability and metrics:
- Emit per-tx metrics: fetch_time_per_shard, validate_time, apply_latency, commit_latency, tx_success/failure, disk_bytes_moved, active_epoch
- Emit KV-staleness metrics: fraction of requests using stale-KV, new-epoch-warmup-rate
- Traces: mark critical path spans for fetch, validate, apply for distributed tracing.

Testing and verification checklist:
- Unit tests for idempotent journal replay logic
- Integration tests simulating crashes at each step (prepare/fetch/validate/apply/commit)
- Perf tests for phased canary applying to 1000 hosts and measuring tail latencies
- Chaos tests: disk full, flakey network, corrupted shard blob

Operational playbook (short):
- How to abort a rollout: controller writes abort_<txid> and nodes that see an abort will stop APPLY and cleanup temp files; committed txs are not reverted automatically.
- Rollback: create compensating tx that re-activates previous artifact versions with a new tx_id and rely on controller quorum semantics for rapid reversion.
- Emergency recovery: if many nodes are stuck mid-apply, run a coordinated "replay sweep" that forces journal replay and reports per-node status to controller.

Open questions / future work:
- Should we include a compact consensus step (RAFT/etcd) for tx ordering in stricter enterprise deployments, or is eventual consistent log sufficient for most rollouts?
- Can we leverage hardware snapshots (NVMe snapshots) to make APPLY faster and safer for very large artifacts?
- Explore delta-encoding of shard diffs to reduce fetch bandwidth for minor weight updates.

Appendix: lightweight API sketches (informal):
- Controller -> publish_tx(manifest) -> returns tx_id
- Node -> tail_log(since_tx_id) -> stream of manifests
- Node -> report_status(tx_id, state, details) -> controller aggregates

Summary of benefits:
- Clear crash-recovery semantics and idempotent local operations reduce risk of inconsistent state during rollouts.
- Allows incremental, bandwidth-efficient fetch strategies while keeping activation atomic at serving time.
- Decouples KV cache semantics via epoch tagging instead of wholesale invalidation, reducing cold-start cost after upgrades.

Next steps:
- Prototype local activation journal and simple controller that publishes manifests to S3 + SNS for notifications (2 week spike)
- End-to-end chaos testing on staging fleet
